answer:
For a chemical reaction the enthalpy change \(\Delta H\) and the internal energy change \(\Delta U\) are related through the definition of enthalpy.

By definition,

\(H = U + PV\)

For a change from an initial state 1 to a final state 2,

\(H_2 - H_1 = (U_2 - U_1) + (P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)\)

\(\therefore \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta(PV)\)

At constant pressure \(P\) this becomes

\(\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V\)

If the gaseous reactants and products behave ideally, and \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) are the numbers of moles of gaseous reactants and gaseous products at the same temperature \(T\),

\(PV_1 = n_1RT\) and \(PV_2 = n_2RT\)

\(\therefore P\Delta V = P(V_2 - V_1) = (n_2 - n_1)RT = \Delta n_{g}RT\)

Substituting this in the previous equation,

\(\therefore \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{g}RT\)

where \(\Delta n_{g} = \) (number of moles of gaseous products) \(-\) (number of moles of gaseous reactants).

For a reaction such as \(\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl(g)}\), \(\Delta n_{g} = 2 - 2 = 0\) and the relation reduces to \(\Delta H = \Delta U\), as it must, because no volume change and hence no expansion work occurs.

For a conductivity cell the conductivity and the measured resistance are related by

\(k = \dfrac{\text{cell constant}}{R}\)

\(\therefore \text{Cell constant} = k \times R\)

Here \(k = 1.46 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\) and \(R = 1500\ \Omega\), and \(1\ \mathrm{S} = 1\ \Omega^{-1}\).

\(\text{Cell constant} = 1.46 \times 10^{-4}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} \times 1500\ \Omega\)

\(\therefore \text{Cell constant} = 0.219\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

Check: the cell constant is the ratio \(l/a\) of the separation of the electrodes to the area of cross section of an electrode, so its unit must be \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), and \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} \times \Omega\) leaves exactly that.
twin: A conductivity cell containing 0.01M KCl gives at 25 C the resistance of 604 ohms. The same cell containing 0.001M AgNO3 gives resistance of 6530 ohms. Calculate the molar conductivity of 0.001M AgNO3.

answer:
i. Conductivity of the solution.

\(k = \dfrac{\text{cell constant}}{R} = \dfrac{0.367\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{31.6\ \Omega}\)

\(= 1.161 \times 10^{-2}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

ii. Molar conductivity of the solution.

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\), where \(c = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

\(= \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{cm^3\ L^{-1}} \times 1.161 \times 10^{-2}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}\)

\(\therefore \Lambda = 232.3\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

Check: putting this value back, \(k = \dfrac{\Lambda c}{1000} = \dfrac{232.3 \times 0.05}{1000} = 1.16 \times 10^{-2}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), which is the conductivity obtained in step i.

Molar conductivity and conductivity are related by

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\), that is \(k = \dfrac{\Lambda c}{1000}\)

Here \(\Lambda = 223\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(c = 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\).

\(k = \dfrac{223\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}{1000\ \mathrm{cm^3\ L^{-1}}}\)

\(\therefore k = 0.01115\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

Check: \(\dfrac{1000 \times 0.01115}{0.05} = 223\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\), the molar conductivity given.

Molar conductivity is obtained from the conductivity by

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\)

Here \(k = 0.01\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) and \(c = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\).

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\ \mathrm{cm^3\ L^{-1}} \times 0.01\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{0.5\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}\)

\(\therefore \Lambda = 20\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

Check: \(k = \dfrac{\Lambda c}{1000} = \dfrac{20 \times 0.5}{1000} = 0.01\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\), the conductivity given.

answer:
The SI unit of molar conductivity is \(\mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}}\).

It follows from the defining relation. Molar conductivity is the conductance of the volume \(V\) of solution containing one mole of the electrolyte, so

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{k}{c}\)

In SI units the conductivity \(k\) is measured in \(\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}\) and the concentration \(c\) in \(\mathrm{mol\ m^{-3}}\). Hence

\(\Lambda = \dfrac{\mathrm{S\ m^{-1}}}{\mathrm{mol\ m^{-3}}} = \mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

In laboratory work the same quantity is conveniently expressed in \(\Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\), and \(1\ \mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}} = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).

The calomel electrode is a secondary reference electrode, represented as \(\mathrm{Hg(l)\,|\,Hg_2Cl_2(s)\,|\,KCl(aq)}\). The labelled diagram is drawn as follows.

- A **glass tube** closed at the bottom, standing upright.
- A small pool of **pure mercury**, \(\mathrm{Hg(l)}\), lying at the bottom of the tube.
- A **platinum wire** dipping into the mercury and sealed through the glass, its upper end brought out as the **terminal** for connection to the external circuit.
- Immediately above the mercury, a layer of **paste of mercury and mercurous chloride** (calomel, \(\mathrm{Hg_2Cl_2}\)).
- Above the paste, the tube filled with a **solution of potassium chloride** of fixed concentration - 0.1 M, 1 M or saturated - which is the electrolyte.
- A **side tube at the top**, through which the \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution is filled.
- A **second side tube** at the lower side, ending in a porous plug or drawn out as a **salt bridge**, through which the electrode is connected to the other half cell.

The electrode reaction, when the electrode acts as the cathode, is

\(\mathrm{Hg_2Cl_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Hg(l)} + 2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus(aq)}\)

Its potential depends only on the concentration of \(\mathrm{KCl}\) and stays constant at a fixed temperature, and it has been measured accurately against the standard hydrogen electrode (\(0.2422\ \mathrm{V}\) with saturated \(\mathrm{KCl}\) at \(298\ \mathrm{K}\)). That constant, known value is what allows it to serve as a reference electrode.

The lead storage battery (lead accumulator) is drawn and labelled as follows.

- A **container** of hard rubber or polypropylene, which is not attacked by acid.
- The **electrolyte**, an aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) of about 38% by mass, filling the container.
- The **anode**, marked negative \((-)\): a set of lead grid plates packed with **spongy lead**, \(\mathrm{Pb}\).
- The **cathode**, marked positive \((+)\): a set of lead grid plates packed with **lead dioxide**, \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\).
- The two kinds of plate arranged **alternately**, kept apart by **insulating separators** of wood or fibre glass so that they cannot touch.
- All the lead plates joined together and all the lead dioxide plates joined together, that is the plates of each kind connected in **parallel**, and the two groups brought out as the **negative and positive terminals** at the top.

Each such cell gives about 2 V, and six cells connected in **series** make the 12 V battery used in a motor car.

**(B)** \(\mathrm{KOH}\)

In the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell both electrodes are porous carbon rods containing a small amount of finely divided platinum as a catalyst. They are immersed in **hot aqueous potassium hydroxide**, which is the electrolyte; hydrogen gas is bubbled through the anode and oxygen gas through the cathode.

Oxidation at the anode \((-)\):

\(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Reduction at the cathode \((+)\):

\(\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

Both electrode reactions are written in terms of \(\mathrm{OH^\ominus}\) ions, which the electrolyte must therefore supply and regenerate. An acid, or the solution of a neutral salt, contains no appreciable concentration of hydroxide ions and cannot sustain these reactions.

answer:
**What a fuel cell is.** A galvanic cell in which the chemical energy of the combustion of a fuel, such as hydrogen, methane or methanol, is converted directly into electrical energy is called a fuel cell. The fuel and the oxidant are not stored inside the cell but are supplied continuously from outside, so the cell does not run down and needs no recharging; it goes on working as long as the supply of fuel lasts.

The commonest example is the hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, in which both electrodes are porous carbon rods containing finely divided platinum as a catalyst, immersed in hot aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\).

**Anode reaction (oxidation).** Hydrogen gas is bubbled through the anode \((-)\), where it is oxidised to water.

\(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

**Cathode reaction (reduction).** Oxygen gas is bubbled through the cathode \((+)\), where it is reduced to hydroxide ions.

\(\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

**Net cell reaction.** Adding the two electrode reactions, the electrons and the hydroxide ions cancel:

\(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

so the overall change is simply the combustion of hydrogen to water, although the fuel and the oxidant never come into direct contact. The cell potential is

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode} = 0.4\ \mathrm{V} - (-0.83\ \mathrm{V}) = 1.23\ \mathrm{V}\)

answer:
The primary reference electrode is the **standard hydrogen electrode (SHE)**, represented as \(\mathrm{Pt\,|\,H_2(g,\ 1\ atm)\,|\,H^\oplus(1\ M)}\). The labelled diagram is drawn as follows.

- An outer **glass tube (jacket)**, open at the bottom, standing in the solution.
- A **platinum wire** sealed through the top of the tube and carrying, at its lower end, a small square of **platinum foil coated with platinum black**. The upper end of the wire is the **terminal** for the external circuit.
- The solution in which the foil dips: **1 M \(\mathrm{H^\oplus}\)**, that is \(1\ \mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{HCl}\).
- A **side inlet tube** at the top through which **pure hydrogen gas at 1 atm** is passed continuously down over the platinum foil, drawn as bubbles rising round the foil.
- **Holes or an opening at the bottom** of the jacket for the excess hydrogen gas to escape into the solution.
- A **salt bridge** leading out of the beaker, connecting this half cell to the other half cell.
- The whole assembly kept at the stated temperature, \(298\ \mathrm{K}\).

The half reaction at the electrode is

\(2\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)

Its potential is **arbitrarily fixed at exactly zero volt** at all temperatures. Because one electrode of the cell then contributes nothing, the measured cell potential is the potential of the other electrode, and every standard electrode potential is quoted on this scale. The platinum black is required because it adsorbs hydrogen gas and catalyses the half reaction, so that the electrode reaches equilibrium quickly and its potential stays steady.

**(A)** \(0.737\ \mathrm{V}\)

In the given reaction \(\mathrm{Cd}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Cd^{2\oplus}}\), so the cadmium electrode is the **anode**, and \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cu}\), so the copper electrode is the **cathode**. The cell is

\(\mathrm{Cd(s)\,|\,Cd^{2\oplus}(aq)\,||\,Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)\,|\,Cu(s)}\)

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode} = E^0_{Cu} - E^0_{Cd}\)

\(= 0.334\ \mathrm{V} - (-0.403\ \mathrm{V})\)

\(\therefore E^0_{cell} = 0.737\ \mathrm{V}\)

Check: cadmium has the more negative standard potential, so it is the stronger reducing agent and displaces copper from its solution. The reaction as written is therefore spontaneous and \(E^0_{cell}\) must come out positive, as it does. The value \(0.069\ \mathrm{V}\) is what subtracting the two magnitudes would give, which ignores the sign of the cadmium potential.

answer:
The \(\mathrm{H_2} - \mathrm{O_2}\) fuel cell is drawn and labelled as follows.

- A **container** holding the electrolyte, which is **hot aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\)** solution.
- Two **porous carbon rod electrodes** containing a small amount of finely divided platinum, which acts as a catalyst, dipping into the electrolyte.
- The left electrode marked **anode \((-)\)**, with an **inlet** through which **hydrogen gas** is bubbled continuously over it.
- The right electrode marked **cathode \((+)\)**, with an **inlet** through which **oxygen gas** is bubbled continuously over it.
- An **outlet** at the top of each compartment for the excess gas, and an outlet for the **water** formed.
- The two electrodes joined through an **external circuit** carrying the load, with the direction of electron flow marked from the anode to the cathode.

The electrode reactions are

anode \((-)\): \(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

cathode \((+)\): \(\mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} + 4\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow 4\mathrm{OH^\ominus(aq)}\)

net: \(2\mathrm{H_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

**Two applications of a fuel cell.**

i. It is used as the source of electric power in **spacecraft**, as in the Apollo space programme; the water produced by the cell is used by the astronauts for drinking.

ii. It is used as a **pollution-free power source for automobiles and for standby electric supply**, its only product being water and its efficiency being about 70% against about 40% for a thermal power plant.

A **reference electrode** is an electrode of accurately known and constant potential, which is combined with a given electrode to form a cell so that the potential of that given electrode can be determined from the measured cell potential.

Such an electrode is needed because every oxidation must be accompanied by a reduction, so a single electrode carries only one half reaction and its potential cannot be measured by itself. What is measured is always the potential of a complete cell, that is the algebraic sum of the potentials of its two electrodes. If one of the two is a reference electrode of known potential, the potential of the other follows at once.

The **standard hydrogen electrode**, \(\mathrm{Pt\,|\,H_2(g,\ 1\ atm)\,|\,H^\oplus(1\ M)}\), whose potential is arbitrarily taken as exactly zero volt, is the **primary** reference electrode. The **calomel** electrode and the **silver - silver chloride** electrode, whose potentials have been measured accurately against it, are **secondary** reference electrodes.

The lead accumulator cell is drawn and labelled as follows.

- A **container** of hard rubber or polypropylene, unattacked by acid.
- The **electrolyte**, an aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) of about 38% by mass.
- The **anode** \((-)\): lead grid plates packed with **spongy lead**, \(\mathrm{Pb}\).
- The **cathode** \((+)\): lead grid plates packed with **lead dioxide**, \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\).
- The plates arranged **alternately** and kept apart by **insulating separators**, the plates of each kind connected in **parallel** and brought out as the **negative and positive terminals**.

**Reactions during discharging.**

Oxidation at the anode \((-)\): spongy lead is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Pb^{2\oplus}}\), which combines with sulphate ions from the acid and is deposited as insoluble lead sulphate.

\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Reduction at the cathode \((+)\): lead dioxide is reduced, again to lead sulphate.

\(\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

Net cell reaction, obtained by adding the two:

\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)

Sulphuric acid is consumed as the cell discharges, so the density of the electrolyte and with it the cell potential fall; each cell delivers about 2 V and the six cells in series about 12 V.

answer:
In the given reaction \(\mathrm{Mg}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\), so the magnesium electrode is the **anode**, and \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Sn}\), so the tin electrode is the **cathode**. The cell is

\(\mathrm{Mg(s)\,|\,Mg^{2\oplus}(0.06\ M)\,||\,Sn^{2\oplus}(0.04\ M)\,|\,Sn(s)}\)

Two electrons pass from \(\mathrm{Mg}\) to \(\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}\), so \(n = 2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}\). The cell potential at the stated concentrations, written here as \(\Delta E\), is given by the Nernst equation, the solids taking unit activity:

\(\Delta E = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{2.303\,RT}{n\mathrm{F}}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}]}{[\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}]}\)

i. The temperature is \(28\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\), that is \(T = 301\ \mathrm{K}\), so

\(\dfrac{2.303\,RT}{\mathrm{F}} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}} \times 301\ \mathrm{K}}{96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.0597\ \mathrm{V}\)

ii. \(\log_{10}\dfrac{0.06}{0.04} = \log_{10} 1.5 = 0.1761\)

iii. \(\Delta E = 2.23\ \mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0.0597\ \mathrm{V}}{2} \times 0.1761 = 2.23\ \mathrm{V} - 0.0053\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(\therefore \Delta E = 2.225\ \mathrm{V}\)

iv. The Gibbs energy change of the cell reaction is

\(\Delta G = -n\mathrm{F}\,\Delta E = -2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus} \times 96500\ \mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus} \times 2.225\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= -429425\ \mathrm{V\,C} = -429425\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(\therefore \Delta G = -429.4\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

**Is the reaction spontaneous?** Yes. \(\Delta E\) is positive and \(\Delta G\) is negative, and both are the conditions for a spontaneous cell reaction.

Check: \([\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}]\) is greater than \([\mathrm{Sn^{2\oplus}}]\), so the logarithm is positive and the cell potential must fall a little below its standard value - and \(2.225\ \mathrm{V}\) is just below \(2.23\ \mathrm{V}\), as expected.

answer:
**Faraday's first law of electrolysis.** The mass of a substance deposited or liberated at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

If \(W\) is the mass deposited and \(Q\) the charge passed,

\(W \propto Q\), that is \(W = ZQ = Z\,I\,t\)

where \(I\) is the current in ampere, \(t\) the time in second and \(Z\) the constant of proportionality, called the electrochemical equivalent of the substance. \(Z\) is the mass deposited by one coulomb of electricity.

**Faraday's second law of electrolysis.** When the same quantity of electricity is passed through the solutions of different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of the substances deposited or liberated at the respective electrodes are directly proportional to their equivalent masses.

If \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) are the masses deposited and \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) the corresponding equivalent masses,

\(\dfrac{W_1}{W_2} = \dfrac{E_1}{E_2}\)

**12 F**

Hydrogen is liberated at the cathode by the half reaction

\(2\mathrm{H^\oplus(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2(g)}\)

so 2 moles of electrons, that is 2 F, liberate 1 mole of \(\mathrm{H_2}\), which is \(2\ \mathrm{g}\). One faraday therefore liberates \(1\ \mathrm{g}\) of hydrogen.

Moles of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) liberated \(= \dfrac{12\ \mathrm{g}}{2\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 6\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Electricity required \(= 6\ \mathrm{mol} \times 2\ \mathrm{F\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\therefore\) Electricity required \(= 12\ \mathrm{F}\)

Check: \(12\ \mathrm{F}\) is \(12\) moles of electrons, and \(12\) moles of electrons discharge \(12\) moles of \(\mathrm{H^\oplus}\), giving \(6\) moles, that is \(12\ \mathrm{g}\), of \(\mathrm{H_2}\).

Aluminium is deposited at the cathode by the half reaction

\(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al(s)}\)

so 3 moles of electrons, that is \(3\ \mathrm{F}\), are needed for every 1 mole of aluminium.

Moles of \(\mathrm{Al}\) deposited \(= \dfrac{1.5\ \mathrm{F}}{3\ \mathrm{F\ mol^{-1}}}\)

\(\therefore\) Moles of \(\mathrm{Al}\) deposited \(= 0.50\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Check: \(0.50\ \mathrm{mol} \times 27\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}} = 13.5\ \mathrm{g}\). That is the MASS of aluminium deposited, and it appears among the alternatives as though it were a number of moles; the molar mass is given so that the two can be told apart.
twin: How many moles of electrons are required for reduction of 3 moles of Zn2+ to Zn? How many Faradays of electricity will be required?

Aluminium is deposited from \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\) solution at the cathode by

\(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}(aq)} + 3\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Al(s)}\)

so 3 moles of electrons, that is \(3\ \mathrm{F}\), are required for 1 mole \((27.0\ \mathrm{g})\) of aluminium.

Moles of \(\mathrm{Al}\) to be produced \(= \dfrac{13\ \mathrm{g}}{27.0\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.4815\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Electricity required \(= 0.4815\ \mathrm{mol} \times 3\ \mathrm{F\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\therefore\) Electricity required \(= 1.44\ \mathrm{F}\)

Check: \(1.44\ \mathrm{F}\) is \(1.44\) moles of electrons, which deposit \(\dfrac{1.44}{3} = 0.48\) mole of aluminium, that is \(0.48 \times 27.0 = 13\ \mathrm{g}\), the mass asked for.

The balanced equation for the reduction of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) to \(\mathrm{Zn}\) is

\(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn(s)}\)

It shows that 1 mole of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Zn}\) by 2 moles of electrons.

\(\therefore\) For 2 moles of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}}\), \(2 \times 2 = 4\) moles of electrons are required.

One faraday, \(96500\ \mathrm{C}\), is the charge carried by one mole of electrons.

\(\therefore\) For 4 moles of electrons, \(4\ \mathrm{F}\) of electricity is required, that is \(4 \times 96500 = 386000\ \mathrm{C}\).

answer:
i. Stoichiometry at the cathode:

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu(s)}\), so mole ratio \(= \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{mol}}{2\ \mathrm{mol\ e^\ominus}}\)

ii. The mass of the product is

\(W = \dfrac{I\ (\mathrm{A}) \times t\ (\mathrm{s})}{96500\ (\mathrm{C/mol\ e^\ominus})} \times \text{mole ratio} \times \text{molar mass}\)

\(2.4\ \mathrm{g} = \dfrac{2.03\ \mathrm{A} \times t}{96500} \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times 63.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(t = \dfrac{2.4 \times 2 \times 96500}{2.03 \times 63.5} = \dfrac{463200}{128.9}\)

\(\therefore t = 3593\ \mathrm{s} = 59.9\ \mathrm{minutes}\), that is very nearly 1 hour.

Check: \(3593\ \mathrm{s}\) at \(2.03\ \mathrm{A}\) passes \(7294\ \mathrm{C}\), which is \(\dfrac{7294}{96500} = 0.0756\) mole of electrons; half of that, \(0.0378\) mole of \(\mathrm{Cu}\), weighs \(0.0378 \times 63.5 = 2.4\ \mathrm{g}\), the mass required.
twin: What current strength in amperes will be required to produce 2.4 g of Cu from CuSO4 solution in 1 hour? Molar mass of Cu = 63.5 g mol^-1.

Sodium metal is obtained by the reduction of sodium ion at the cathode:

\(\mathrm{Na^\oplus} + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na(s)}\)

so 1 mole of electrons, that is \(96500\ \mathrm{C}\), produces 1 mole \((23\ \mathrm{g})\) of sodium.

Moles of \(\mathrm{Na}\) to be produced \(= \dfrac{1\ \mathrm{g}}{23\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.04348\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Quantity of electricity \(= 0.04348\ \mathrm{mol} \times 96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\therefore\) Quantity of electricity \(= 4196\ \mathrm{C}\), that is \(0.0435\ \mathrm{F}\).

Check: \(4196\ \mathrm{C}\) is \(\dfrac{4196}{96500} = 0.0435\) mole of electrons, which liberates \(0.0435\) mole of sodium, that is \(0.0435 \times 23 = 1.0\ \mathrm{g}\), the mass asked for.

**Definition.** The series obtained by arranging various electrodes, that is various redox couples, in the increasing order of their standard reduction potentials measured against the standard hydrogen electrode is called the electrochemical series or the electromotive series.

**Applications of the electrochemical series.**

i. **Relative strengths of oxidising agents.** The species on the left of the half reactions are oxidising agents, and the larger the standard potential the stronger the oxidising agent. \(\mathrm{F_2}\), at the bottom of the series, is the strongest oxidising agent.

ii. **Relative strengths of reducing agents.** The species on the right of the half reactions are reducing agents, and the more negative the standard potential the stronger the reducing agent. \(\mathrm{Li}\) is the strongest reducing agent.

iii. **Calculation of the standard cell potential.** For a cell built from any two electrodes of the series, \(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode}\), the electrode with the higher standard potential being the cathode.

iv. **Prediction of the spontaneity of a redox reaction.** The reaction occurs spontaneously under standard conditions only if the \(E^0_{cell}\) so calculated is positive. In particular a metal displaces from solution the ion of any metal that stands lower in reducing strength, as \(\mathrm{Zn}\) displaces \(\mathrm{Cu}\) from \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) solution.

v. **Comparison of the reactivity of metals.** A metal with a more negative standard potential loses electrons more readily and is the more reactive of the two.

**Electrometallurgy** is the extraction of a metal from its fused (molten) salt or ore by electrolysis.

Highly reactive metals such as sodium, potassium, magnesium, calcium and aluminium are themselves strong reducing agents, so their compounds cannot be reduced to the metal by the ordinary reducing agents such as carbon. Instead their molten compounds are electrolysed, and the metal ion is reduced to the metal by electrons supplied at the cathode.

For example, in the electrolysis of molten \(\mathrm{NaCl}\):

cathode: \(\mathrm{Na^\oplus(l)} + \mathrm{e^\ominus} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na(l)}\)

anode: \(2\mathrm{Cl^\ominus(l)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cl_2(g)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Aluminium is obtained in the same way, by the electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite. The mass of metal obtained is governed by Faraday's laws, so the process is worked out from the current and the time for which it is passed.

**a. Electrochemical series.** The series obtained by arranging various electrodes, that is various redox couples, in the increasing order of their standard reduction potentials measured against the standard hydrogen electrode is called the electrochemical series or the electromotive series.

**b. Corrosion.** The slow eating away of a metal by the chemical or electrochemical attack of its surroundings - moist air, water, acids or salt solutions - with the formation of compounds such as oxides, hydroxides, sulphides or carbonates, is called corrosion. The rusting of iron, in which hydrated iron(III) oxide is formed, is the commonest example.

**Two applications of the electrochemical series.**

i. **Relative strengths of oxidising and reducing agents.** The species on the left of the half reactions are oxidising agents and become stronger as the standard potential increases; the species on the right are reducing agents and become stronger as the standard potential becomes more negative.

ii. **Prediction of the spontaneity of a redox reaction.** For any two electrodes of the series, \(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{cathode} - E^0_{anode}\), and the reaction occurs spontaneously under standard conditions only if this comes out positive. Thus zinc displaces copper from \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) solution, the standard potential of the \(\mathrm{Zn^{2\oplus}\,|\,Zn}\) electrode being \(-0.76\ \mathrm{V}\) and that of the \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}\,|\,Cu}\) electrode \(+0.34\ \mathrm{V}\), because \(E^0_{cell} = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10\ \mathrm{V}\).
